lines.text: St. Luke 18: 9-14
August 4, 1940
He also told this parable to some who trusted in themselves that
they were righteous and despised others: "Two men went up into
the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector.
The Pharisee stood and prayed thus with himself, 'God, I thank
thee that 1 am not like other men, extortioners, unjust, adulterers,
or even like this tax collector. I tast twice a week, - give tithes of
all that I get.' But the tax collector, standing far off, would not
even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying, 'God,
be merciful to me a sinner!' I tell you, this man went down to his
house justified rather than the other; for every one who exalts
himself will be humbled, but he who humbles himself will be
exalted."
I
THe story of the Pharisee and the Publican may seem to us a
very simple one which everybody can understand immedi-
ately, and the truth of which is transparently clear to all.
And yet we ought to guard against the danger of taking it
in too simple a sense and regarding its truth too much as a
matter of course. Certainly in detail there is little to explain.
The story is not strictly speaking a parable; for nothing is
here compared. Parable is here used, as often in the New
Testament, in a broad sense, that of an instructive story
simply; and the story presents the contrasting figures of the
Pharisee and the Publican as types so that we should ask
ourselves: which of these types do we resemble? The
Pharisee is the model of correct and zealous piety which in
its observance of the law does too much rather than too
little; the Publican is a despised figure who stands in close
relation with foreigners, with Romans, and lives a dubious
existence commonly disparaged as a life of fraud and
